decisions.reason: SOL keeps the timing; “that day” fits the past-tense narration.
SOL preserves the border encounter in more direct wording.
SOL keeps the gleaming eyes and fully covered armor in natural English.
The Korean describes a dragon on the golden flag; SOL changes it to multiple dragons.
SOL keeps the Son of Heaven as the guards’ sole master without the redundant Emperor reference.
The Korean asks whether they meant the shout, so singular “it” fits.
SOL preserves the question of whether even one guard meant it.
The Korean says the master raises or keeps beasts; “keeps us” drops the raising image.
SOL preserves the Son of Heaven’s supremacy and power over life and death.
SOL continues the preceding thought without changing the carriage’s direction.
SOL preserves the disguise and change into brocade and armor in cleaner phrasing.
The Korean says the commoners prostrated themselves; SOL preserves that physical action.
SOL keeps the half-day journey and routes cleared for them alone.
SOL preserves the wall and Hong Jin’s resolve in the same fragmentary, reflective voice.
The Korean describes a sigh, not a gasp.
The Korean says it was someone’s cold voice; SOL identifies it as “that” voice.
SOL keeps the sunset spreading from the west and staining the walls.
The Korean explicitly describes an abundance of goods; SOL drops that quantity.
“Broad” preserves the plains’ wide expanse without changing the image.
SOL turns the fragment into natural English while keeping the remembered saying and its truth.
“Ominous” preserves the city’s threatening atmosphere in natural narration.
“Blades” fits the cold scraping sound of the armed soldiers’ weapons.
SOL preserves the contrast with half-trained grunts and the troops’ elite readiness.
The following dialogue supplies the speech; SOL keeps the meaningful loss of Mujin’s smile.
Removing “But” does not change the contrast or the narrator’s agreement.
SOL keeps the escalation from many soldiers to a downright disgusting number.
SOL keeps the Longjing tea and Imperial Guards exaggeration without a redundant setup.
The context makes clear that Hong Jin is answering the narrator’s question.
“But” preserves the contrast between routine security and this exceptional deployment.
The Korean says Hong Jin licked his lips and murmured; SOL drops the murmuring cue.
SOL keeps Hong Jin’s suspicion and the excessive welcome in idiomatic dialogue.
SOL resolves “him” as Prince Shangshan Zhu Bao without changing the claim.
SOL preserves the younger-brother relationship and the requirement for public justification.
The emperor is the clear antecedent, so “his” keeps the meaning without repetition.
SOL preserves the point that the saying about popular will and Heaven has a reason.
SOL preserves the fall of the steppe rulers as popular support crumbled.
SOL keeps the negative public view and its connection to the preceding point.
SOL preserves what the narrator had heard in Murim and learned from Hong Jin.
SOL keeps the emperor’s military record and reputation for meticulous governance.
The context identifies “he” as the emperor; SOL keeps both conditions for inheriting the throne.
The Korean says he was far from the line of succession, not merely far from the throne.
SOL clarifies that the Crown Prince was outstanding compared with his younger brother.
“Benevolence and integrity” preserves the Korean praise and reads naturally.
SOL preserves that both the rebellion’s seeds and the foreign threats were uprooted.
The Korean’s 적통 is rendered by the established “orthodox lineage”; SOL replaces that specific succession concept with a claim to the throne.
SOL preserves the fourth son’s position outside succession and his drawing a sword from the shadows.
SOL keeps the unusually clear hoofbeats snapping the narrator out of his thoughts.
SOL preserves the stopped carriage and the unfamiliar buildings beyond the packed guards.
SOL keeps the skyscraper comparison and the palace buildings’ unmatched splendor.
SOL preserves the overwhelming palace entrance and the whispered approach without adding that the narrator felt small.
“Held off asking” naturally conveys Hong Jin holding back his question until now.
SOL keeps the narrator’s immediate understanding of what Hong Jin meant.
The sentence is retained in H054, so this deletion avoids duplication rather than dropping content.
SOL retains the journey sentence here and preserves the point that mistrust would increase anxiety and danger.
SOL keeps the transition to the narrator’s own question.
“How do you know so much?” preserves the question about Hong Jin’s extensive knowledge.
SOL keeps the long-standing question in natural English.
“Direct member of the imperial family” preserves the source’s direct imperial kinship.
SOL keeps the trusted-aide context, breadth of knowledge, and calm dealings with the guards.
“Doing it like this” preserves the narrator’s need to ask directly by Sound Transmission.
The Korean says he must hear an answer to this question; SOL weakens that demand to needing an answer and adds “too.”
SOL preserves the firm Sound Transmission, Hong Jin’s silent stare, and his opening the door.
SOL keeps the group descending from the palace and Hong Jin speaking to them.
“Unable to bear his hunger” naturally preserves the boy’s inability to endure starvation.
SOL keeps Hong Jin’s desire to leave the sewer for the wide, clear sea.
The Korean says Hong Jin had the ability to fulfill his ambitions; “pursue” weakens that claim.
“Unfailing thoroughness” preserves the sense of his consistently meticulous character.
The split sentence preserves the late Emperor’s summons and what he told Hong Jin.
SOL preserves the clear quality of Hong Jin’s voice without redundant narration.
SOL uses the project’s ellipsis character while preserving the shocked reaction.
